prime.problem: Without a clear target, the next 17 cards are a pile of pieces: embeddings, heads, residuals, LayerNorm. You need to know what the finished model does, what it reads, and how its quality is scored, or you can't tell whether a piece helped.
prime.fits: First card of the GPT lecture. It reuses the language-modelling setup from the makemore courses (predict the next character, score it with negative log likelihood), swapping the names dataset for 1.1M characters of Shakespeare.
expect: a language model as a next-character predictor
the generation loop: predict, sample, append
validation loss as the score, from 4.17 down to 1.48
prime.goal: Explain what a character-level GPT computes at each step, load tiny Shakespeare and print its length and vocabulary, and read any loss in this course as a point on the 4.17 → 1.48 ladder.

attend: Why does the model output 65 probabilities rather than one character, and where does the randomness in the writing come from?
What does the uniform-guess loss of 4.17 assume the model knows, and what does each later rung on the ladder add?
Why is eloss easier to picture than the loss itself?
What do we gain and give up by using characters instead of GPT-2's sub-word tokens?
Why can't a count table like makemore's scale to eight characters of context?

must: The model outputs a probability for each of the 65 characters → we sample one and append it → the new text becomes the next context → repeating this writes text of any length (and differs each run, because the draw is random)

Loss is the average −ln of the probability given to the true next character → a model that knows nothing gives 1/65 everywhere → loss −ln(1/65) = 4.17 is the floor to beat → every piece added in this course is judged by how far it pushes val loss toward 1.48

Using more context lowers the loss: no context (frequencies only) 3.35 → one previous character 2.49 → 256 characters through a Transformer 1.48 → the whole lecture is about letting the model use more of the past, well

Count tables need one row per possible context → 65<sup>8</sup> ≈ 3.2 × 10<sup>14</sup> rows for 8 characters, far more than 1.1M characters can fill → learned weights that share structure across contexts are the only way to use long context
elevated: Characters give a 65-symbol vocabulary but 3.3× longer sequences than GPT-2 tokens (1,115,394 vs 338,025) → cheap embedding and output layers, but more steps per sentence → real models pick sub-word tokens
reference: tiny Shakespeare input.txt: 1,115,394 characters, 40,000 lines, 202,651 whitespace-split words
chars = sorted(list(set(text))), vocab_size = len(chars) = 65; \n sorts first, space second
the only digit is 3 (27 times); the rarest character is $ (once)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the generation loop as boxes and arrows, then write 3–4 sentences on how its quality is measured and which numbers bracket the course.
checklist: context → model → 65 probabilities → sample → append → repeat
sampling is random, so the same prompt gives different text
loss = average −ln(probability of the true next character), lower is better
uniform guessing gives −ln(1/65) = 4.17; the finished GPT reaches 1.48
more usable context is what moves the loss down

retrieve.q: Explain what a language model is in terms of inputs and outputs, and how it turns into a text generator.
answer: input: the characters so far (the context)
output: a probability for every one of the 65 characters
generator: sample one, append it, feed the longer text back in
repeat for as many characters as you want

retrieve.q: Walk through why a model that has learned nothing scores 4.17, and what e<sup>4.17</sup> means.
answer: it gives every character probability 1/65
every position then contributes −ln(1/65) = 4.1744, so the average is the same
e<sup>4.1744</sup> = 65: as unsure as picking among all 65 at random

retrieve.q: Walk through what changes at each rung of the ladder 3.35 → 2.49 → 1.48, in terms of what the model is allowed to look at.
answer: 3.35: no context, only how common each character is
2.49: the previous character (bigram)
1.48: up to 256 previous characters through attention
each rung sees more of the past, so the true next character gets more probability

retrieve.q: You're building a model for this 1 MB file. Choose between characters and GPT-2 sub-word tokens, and name the cost of each.
answer: characters: 65 symbols, no tokenizer, any string representable
characters cost: 1,115,394 steps of text vs 338,025, so context covers less text
GPT-2 tokens: 50,257-symbol vocab, large embedding and output layers for so little data
for learning how a Transformer works, characters win; for real models, sub-words do

compare.q: Both courses train a character-level model to predict the next character. What is fundamentally different about the data and the model, and how does each one fail?
answer: names: 32k short words, each its own sequence with start/end tokens; Shakespeare: one 1.1M-character stream
the bigram sees one previous character; the GPT sees up to 256
the bigram fails by forgetting everything before the last character
the GPT fails by overfitting or running slowly as context grows, which the later cards address

compare.q: This card calls our model 'the first half of a tiny ChatGPT'. Which design choice makes it only half, and what fails if you ask it a question?
answer: ours is pretrained only: it learns to continue text
ChatGPT adds fine-tuning so it answers like an assistant
asked a question, ours just continues with Shakespeare-shaped text

predict.q: The frequency-only model scores 3.35 on validation using counts from the training split. Suppose instead you counted the frequencies on the validation text itself and then scored the validation text. Commit to a guess: higher, lower or the same, and roughly by how much?
predict.answer: Slightly lower, but only a little: 3.3373 vs 3.3473. Counting on the text you're scored on is cheating (it has peeked at the answers), yet with no context there's so little to overfit that the gain is tiny. Cheating like this becomes a real problem once a model has millions of parameters and can memorise; that's why the next card holds back 10% for validation.

apply.task: Extend labs/shakespeare-lm.py: use collections.Counter to count each character in the first 90% of the text, then compute the average −ln(probability) of each character in the last 10% under those counts. Before running, guess where it lands between 4.17 and 2.49.
apply.done: You print about 3.3473 and can say why it sits between uniform guessing (4.1744) and the bigram (2.49): it knows which characters are common, but nothing about order.
apply.hint: Split at n = int(0.9*len(text)). Each character's probability is its count divided by the length of the first part (1,003,854).

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the 65-character vocabulary, or how little counting on the validation text helped?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why loss uses −ln, or what e<sup>loss</sup> means?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: more context → lower loss, or lower loss → better-sounding text?
Could you explain to a friend why ChatGPT isn't just this model scaled up?
Which number will you use to judge each piece you add on the coming cards?
